hints: Start with Fig. 1.1 and trace the normal direction of an impulse - from the branched receiving end on the left, through the large cell body, along the axon to the branched releasing end on the right.

Think about what each region does - the branched extensions that collect signals, the central structure in the cell body that holds DNA and controls the cell, and the swollen tips at the end that store vesicles.
Use the precise syllabus names - A is the plural branching fibres on the cell body, B is the control centre containing chromosomes, C is the swollen presynaptic endings.
walkthrough:
Map the Neurone From Input to Output**
Imagine you are a signal travelling through. You arrive at the many fine branches around the cell body on the left, you pass through the large cell body in the middle, then you travel down the long axon and leave from the tiny swellings on the right. That left to right logic helps you place each label.

Assign Each Label**
A points to the branched fibres extending from the cell body that receive stimuli and carry graded potentials toward the cell body. These are dendrites. B points to the round structure inside the cell body containing DNA that controls protein synthesis and metabolism. This is the nucleus. C points to the swollen tips at the end of the axon branches that contain synaptic vesicles for release of transmitter. These are synaptic knobs.
Final answer: A = dendrites; B = nucleus (nuclei); C = synaptic knobs.

hints: Compare the two axons carefully in Fig. 1.1. One has regular blocks wrapped around it and a much smaller diameter ($7 \mu m$ vs $40 \mu m$), yet it is faster ($50 m s^{-1}$ vs $8 m s^{-1}$). Which feature must be dominating over diameter?
Recall how that wrapping made by Schwann cells changes where action potentials can form, so the impulse does not have to be regenerated at every point along the membrane.
walkthrough:
Spot the Key Structural Difference**
The snail has a very wide axon of diameter $40 \mu m$ which alone would normally speed up conduction by reducing resistance. The rat has a narrow axon of only $7 \mu m$, but its axon is wrapped in Schwann cells forming a myelin sheath with gaps. Myelin is a fatty insulator.

Link Myelin to Saltatory Conduction**
Myelin prevents ion movement and action potential formation across the insulated regions. Voltage-gated $Na^+$ and $K^+$ channels are concentrated at the nodes of Ranvier between Schwann cells. Local circuits therefore jump rapidly from node to node, called saltatory conduction. This is much faster than continuous propagation along the unmyelinated snail axon, so the rat reaches $50 m s^{-1}$ compared to $8 m s^{-1}$ in the snail.
Final answer: Rat neurone is myelinated with myelin sheath / Schwann cells; impulse undergoes saltatory conduction, jumping from one node of Ranvier to the next.

hints: Lay Fig. 1.2 (rat) and Fig. 1.3 (snail) side by side. Check the axes are identical - membrane potential in $mV$ against time in $ms$ - so you can compare heights and widths directly like with like.
First compare how high each spike goes above $0 mV$. Then compare how wide each spike is and how quickly each returns to the resting level of about $-40 mV$.
Finally look below the resting line at the dip and how long the trace stays disturbed before flattening. Think about what a longer spike means for refractory period and frequency of firing.
walkthrough:
Compare Peak Depolarisation**
Both start at a resting potential of about $-40 mV$. The rat depolarises to a peak of about $+25 mV$ at about $7 ms$. The snail depolarises more strongly to a peak of about $+45 mV$ at about $6 ms$. So the snail shows greater depolarisation and a more positive peak.

Compare Speed and Duration**
The rat spike is narrow and fast. It repolarises back to $-40 mV$ by about $11-12 ms$, lasting only about $6-7 ms$ in total. The snail spike is broad and slow. It repolarises gradually back to $-40 mV$ only by about $20 ms$, lasting about $17-18 ms$. The snail therefore takes longer to complete the action potential.

Compare Recovery and Hyperpolarisation**
After the spike both dip below $-40 mV$ into hyperpolarisation. In the rat the dip to about $-52 mV$ is brief, returning to rest by about $13 ms$. In the snail the dip to about $-50 mV$ is prolonged, not returning to rest until about $26 ms$. That means the snail has a longer hyperpolarisation phase and a longer absolute and relative refractory period, so it cannot fire as frequently.

Final answer: Snail (Fig. 1.3) compared to rat (Fig. 1.2): greater depolarisation to higher peak, about $+45 mV$ vs about $+25 mV$; slower action potential, takes longer to return to resting potential, about $20 ms$ vs about $7-8 ms$; longer refractory period / longer hyperpolarisation phase.
